config.title: Berlin Club Dress Codes - FAQ
config.subtitle: What each Berlin door actually screens for, why almost none of them publish a dress code, the phone sticker rule, and which venues are still open at the hour you plan to arrive.

items.q: Is there a dress code for Berlin clubs?
items.a: **At almost every serious Berlin club, no published one exists.** Berghain, Tresor, Sisyphos, ://about blank, RSO, Kater and Renate all select at the door and none of them prints a rule you can read in advance. The reliable pattern is that dark, plain, comfortable clothes read as normal because that is what the room already wears, not because it is a requirement. The two exceptions are KitKatClub, which does publish and enforce a dress rule and refuses street clothes, and Matrix at Warschauer Straße, which runs an ordinary commercial smart-casual door.

items.q: What is the Tresor Berlin dress code?
items.a: **There is no official Tresor dress code.** You do not need black, designer clothes or anything fetish. What the door is actually reading is your group size, how sober you look and how you behave in the queue. Tresor does publish two house rules that matter more than your outfit: photography and filming inside are not allowed and guests who do it are removed, and the cloakroom is self-service, so bring a charged phone with NFC switched on. Tresor sits in the Kraftwerk on Köpenicker Straße near U Heinrich-Heine-Straße and runs Friday and Saturday nights from around midnight.

items.q: Why does the Berlin door reject people who look fine?
items.a: **Because the outfit is the smallest part of what is being read.** A door working at capacity is choosing who makes the room better for the people already inside. Groups of six get split or turned away, loud English gets noticed across a quiet queue, phones out in the line get noticed, and visible drunkenness ends it. None of that is about clothes, which is why the most common visitor mistake is to fix the outfit and change nothing else. Arriving as one or two people, staying quiet, and knowing which night you came for does more than anything you can wear.

items.q: Do Berlin clubs really put stickers on your phone camera?
items.a: **Yes, at most of the ones you have heard of.** Berghain, Tresor, Sisyphos, ://about blank, Kater and Renate all cover phone camera lenses with a sticker at the door. It is not theatre. The no-photo rule is what lets people behave freely inside, and peeling the sticker off is one of the few things that will get you removed and banned rather than warned. Matrix and the smaller open-air bars do not bother, which tells you a lot about what kind of room you are walking into.

items.q: Which Berlin clubs have an easy door?
items.a: **Club der Visionäre and Else, both on the water in Treptow, have effectively no door at all.** They are open-air, they start in the afternoon and they run on summer weather, which also means they are completely shut in winter. Kater on Holzmarktstraße and Ritter Butzke in Kreuzberg are relaxed but popular, so the real cost there is queue length rather than rejection. If a hard door has just said no and you still want the night to be good, walking to one of the water venues is the move that actually works.

items.q: Is Watergate still open in Berlin?
items.a: **No. Watergate closed permanently at the end of 2024**, after 22 years on the Spree next to the Oberbaumbrücke. Its founder cited inflation, energy costs and the rent on that riverside site. The label and brand continue but the club room is gone, and plenty of guidebooks and older blog posts have not caught up. Salon zur Wilden Renate came close to the same ending, announced closure for the end of 2025, then secured its lease in December 2025 and is still running in Alt-Stralau.

items.q: What time should you arrive at a Berlin club?
items.a: **Later than you think, and the quiet hours are the useful ones.** Berlin club nights routinely run from Friday night to Monday, so the crush is roughly midnight to 04:00 on Saturday and Sunday, which is exactly when the queues are longest and the doors are hardest. Sunday afternoon and Monday morning are still inside the same party at Berghain, Sisyphos and Kater, with a fraction of the queue. Turning up at 01:00 on a Saturday with five friends is the single most reliable way to be turned away.

items.q: How much do Berlin clubs cost to get in?
items.a: **Roughly 15 to 30 euro at the door for the big rooms,** with Kater usually in the 20 to 25 euro range and paid on arrival rather than online. Bring cash. Berlin nightlife is one of the last corners of the city where card is not guaranteed, and a cash machine hunt at 02:00 in Schöneweide is a bad end to an evening. Cloakroom is a separate charge almost everywhere, and at Tresor it now runs self-service through your phone.
